newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST-BAe H1 profits seen gaining height.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-BAe H1 profits seen gaining height.

text.p: British Aerospace Plc is expected to confirm the upbeat mood which was in evidence around its headquarters next to the Farnborough air show this week, with strong half-year results next Thursday.
"Most people expect the numbers to be good," said one analyst on Friday. "The company was in chipper mood at Farnborough this week," he added.
The share price has climbed to record highs this week touching 10.23 stg on Friday before falling back under the weight of a generally lower market to 10.12 stg a share.

With the worst of losses from restructuring behind it, analysts say they expect the aircraft and arms giant to come in with underlying profits before tax and non-recurring items of around 180 million stg for the six months to end-June, up from 145 million stg for the same period a year ago.
A restorative 20 to 30 percent boost in the interim dividend payout is likely to be made, to 6-6.5p a share from 5p last time, to indicate the firm's confidence.
A bewildering array of exceptional items usually frustrates attempts to compare headline results with previous years, leaving the dividend as the best gauge.

"People are looking for a punchy increase in the dividend," said Mustapha Omar, industry analyst at stockbrokers Collins Stewart, who expects a 6.5p payout. "Their cover is quite high at about four times (earnings)," he said.

Last year the company paid a total year dividend of 12.5 pence net on earnings of 27.4p. But 1995 results carried several exceptional charges and earnings this year are forecast to bounce up to around 65p a share, going on towards 80 pence a share in 1997.
Analysts say that BAe has cut losses at its turboprop aircraft business thanks to heavy rationalisation and closures,
leaving profits and cash to flow again from arms sales and from its stake in Europe's Airbus Industrie consortium.

The rationalisation of the commercial aerospace division since the crisis days of 1992 has left BAe with a streamlined operation, which analysts say is now paying off with improved margins, particulalry at its core Airbus wing-making operations where turnover is set to take off due to deliveries of bigger aircraft and the general upturn in passenger jet orders.
"Strong trading in BAe's defence division and a sharper than expected revival in the commercial aerospace division implies further upside for the share price," said Omar.
